prompt:
You are a senior information designer and editorial typographer who sets data tables for high-quality publications (statistical yearbooks, reference works, financial reports, technical documentation) in many writing systems, including Chinese. You judge by looking at the real rendered result.

Judge a table layout on all of these levels, in this order of necessity but as one whole:
1. correctness — every character visible, structure intact, nothing clipped or overlapping;
2. readability — natural line breaks, words/numbers/identifiers/semantic units kept whole, continuous reading;
3. function — easy to look up, compare, locate and understand the information for this table's real reading tasks;
4. visual order — alignment, grouping, hierarchy, consistent scale for elements with the same role;
5. visual rhythm — proportion, density changes, distribution of white space, spatial relationships;
6. overall aesthetics — balance, restraint, naturalness, harmony.
Do not assume that equal widths, symmetry, minimum height, the fewest lines, the golden ratio or any fixed proportion is good in itself; decide from this table's function, content and reading task, and look for counter-examples to your own rules.

Table: [val] Co-bottleneck · Framework trade-offs (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Measured content facts (text px at 15px font, padding excluded):
  col 1: header "Option" · longest unbreakable unit 66px · widest one-line content 115px
  col 2: header "Strengths" · longest unbreakable unit 81px · widest one-line content 611px
  col 3: header "Weaknesses" · longest unbreakable unit 90px · widest one-line content 729px
  col 4: header "Verdict" · longest unbreakable unit 52px · widest one-line content 52px
Each column adds 21px of padding+border to its text width.
Viewport: 360px wide (dashed pink box in the renders). At 360px some words cannot fit unsplit. Horizontal scrolling is ALLOWED: the table may be wider than 360px (column widths summing to more than 359px) (the reader scrolls), or you may fit within 359px and accept the consequences. Fitting and scrolling layouts are judged as two separate classes; propose good layouts of BOTH kinds.
Rendering convention: a full render shows the WHOLE table; anything right of the dashed box is not clipped — it is reached by scrolling. Where a layout scrolls, an extra "viewport view" image shows only what is visible at first sight.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. Only the column widths are designed; row heights follow from them.

Your understanding: {"purpose":"Compare three web rendering options and their trade-offs to support a choice.","tasks":["Find an option and read its strengths, weaknesses and verdict across the row.","Compare strengths and weaknesses down their respective columns.","Scan verdicts, then read the supporting trade-offs before deciding.","Read each trade-off as a continuous sentence."],"relations":["Each row connects one option to its advantages, disadvantages and recommendation.","Strengths and weaknesses are paired explanations for the verdict.","Verdicts are short labels; their meaning depends on the trade-offs in the same row."],"roles":["Option names identify the rows.","Strengths and Weaknesses contain the main explanatory text and deserve most of the width.","Verdict is a compact decision aid.","The header labels the four distinct functions consistently across all rows."],"keep_whole":["Individual words, especially option names and column headers where space permits.","Short verdict labels and technical terms such as SEO, CDN and SPA."],"may_wrap":["Multiword option names may wrap between words.","Trade-off sentences may wrap naturally between words and at punctuation."],"same_scale":["Strengths and Weaknesses should have comparable widths because readers compare them, with some extra room for the longer weaknesses.","Option and Verdict are both identification aids, though Option needs more room for its longer labels."],"h_vs_v":"A viewport-fitting table keeps every column visible but forces narrow prose, tall rows and some broken words. Scrolling allows natural wrapping and shorter rows, but readers must move horizontally to connect the option and verdict."}

Image 1 is the one-line content overview. Then real browser renders of: d1r0A, d1r0B (full view, then viewport view), d1r0C (full view, then viewport view).
Measured facts:
d1r0A: column widths [87, 96, 103, 73] px · table 360×797 px · row heights [60, 269, 246, 222] · column headers on >1 line: 1/4 · tallest cell 11 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 4 · fits the 360 px viewport (no scrolling)
d1r0B: column widths [110, 160, 180, 73] px · table 524×425 px · row heights [36, 153, 129, 106] · column headers on >1 line: 0/4 · tallest cell 6 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0 · WIDER than the viewport by 164 px (horizontal scrolling)
d1r0C: column widths [136, 300, 330, 73] px · table 840×262 px · row heights [36, 83, 83, 60] · column headers on >1 line: 0/4 · tallest cell 3 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0 · WIDER than the viewport by 480 px (horizontal scrolling)

Look at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design: what works, what is visually wrong, and the cause (which width). This is your first look at real renders: propose at least one improved or alternative design (refine the most promising, fix what you saw, or test an important idea you have not tried). "done" is not allowed yet. Do not resubmit near-identical widths.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"best":["your best design name(s) so far"],"done":false,"designs":[{"widths":[int px],"change":"what and why"}]}
